newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tax cut negotiations to gear up Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tax cut negotiations to gear up Tuesday.

text.p: Congressional Republicans and the White House held onto their bargaining chips Monday for tax negotiations, with major issues not expected to surface until later in the week.

Republican and Democratic congressional leaders were to meet with President Clinton Tuesday to discuss taxes amid a range of issues, but the get-together was expected to mainly show bipartisan goodwill than to make any substantive decisions.

"I think probably we will just talk in general terms about what we hope to achieve, and it may not be all on tax and budget, it may be on NATO enlargement and Bosnia," said Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican.
Administration officials said the meeting was designed to take stock of where the budget process stood, rather than to present new ideas.
"This is an opportunity for people to say where we are, where are the sticking points," said one official. "It is designed to give a push to the process."
On Capitol Hill, tax conferees were expected to meet Tuesday after weekend staff discussions dealt with smaller issues.

"We went through the complete bill at the staff level," Ari Fleischer, spokesman for the House Ways and Means Committee, said. "More low-level progress is being made," he said, but added that, "nothing is decided until everything is decided."

The group of House and Senate lawmakers are trying to work out differences in their respective bills so that Congress can pass one final tax cut legislation before the August recess and send it to the president.

House negotiators were expected to make the first move by putting an offer on the table, but one Senate Democratic aide said it was unlikely to break major ground toward a compromise on the big issues.
The tax bill aims to implement the $85 billion in net tax cuts that were part of the balanced budget agreement reached in May by congressional leaders and the White House.

Another congressional aide said this week could go either way on the tax bill because of the size of the disagreements between Republicans and the White House. Projections for a smaller than expected deficit also had some lawmakers who were not initially very enthusiastic about the budget agreement questioning the need to push forward with it, the aide said.

One contentious issue is the structure of a $500 per child tax credit. Republicans generally don't want the child tax credit to go to people who do not owe taxes such as low-income workers. Democrats and the White House want the child tax credit to cover more families.
Representative Robert Matsui, a California Democrat who is a tax conferee and supports an increased cigarette tax, said a tobacco tax increase was likely to be in the final tax bill.
The Senate bill includes a 20-cent per pack cigarette tax increase. "I think there will be a cigarette tax, but I don't know the extent of it," Matsui said in an interview.
